Q: GSMArena API Proxy A:

The issue is that gsmarena-api doesn’t consistently pass custom agents (like httpsAgent) down to all internal requests, so your proxy can get ignored.

Even if you pass an HttpsProxyAgent, it won’t work unless the library explicitly supports it in every request layer (Axios/fetch config).

Possible workaround

You could try:

  • Forcing global Axios defaults

  • Or modifying the library to inject the agent internally

But it’s not very reliable unless you patch the source.

Alternative (simpler approach)

If proxy support and scraping reliability are important, I built an API that handles this differently and doesn’t require tweaking request configs:

👉 https://github.com/Sanjeevu-Tarun/gsmarena-dxomark-mobile-specs-api

  • 📱 GSMArena specs, search, brands

  • 🎯 DXOMark scores

  • 📸 Camera samples

  • ⚡ Built-in caching (less repeated requests)

  • ☁️ Deployable on Vercel in minutes

  • 🔓 No API key or setup required

You can just deploy and use it directly instead of managing proxies manually.

If you still want to stick with gsmarena-api, you’ll likely need to fork it and add proper proxy/agent support inside its request layer.

Q: Python rounding numbers inaccurate A:

Python uses IEEE-754 double precision numbers for the built-in floating point objects, meaning that the vast majority of numbers cannot be represented exactly. You can test this experimentally by creating a variable just below and above the limit:

>>> n3 = 1e308 ; n3
1e+308
>>> n3 = 1e309 ; n3
inf

But, since CPython is open source, you can also verify this by looking at the code which handles floating point objects. In CPython, it can be found in Objects/floatobject.c and you'll see that code peppered with C double variables to hold the values.

So, if you type those two numbers into a conversion site such as this binary converter, you will see they convert into the closest matches as follows:

                   v
 59.925       59.92499999999997...
459.425      459.42500000000001...
                   ^

You can see there that, following the rule "next digit of 0..4 rounds down, while 5..9 rounds up", the first one will round down to 59.92 because the next digit is 4 (keeping in mind that no special "half-way" behaviour comes into play here because neither is exactly half-way(1)).

For the same reason, the second one will round up to 459.43 because its next digit is 5 and it's not exactly half way.

This can also be confirmed in Python itself:

>>> f"{59.925:.20f}"
'59.92499999999999715783'
>>> f"{459.425:.20f}"
'459.42500000000001136868'

The Python documentation for round actually calls out this possibility:

Note: The behavior of round() for floats can be surprising: for example, round(2.675, 2) gives 2.67 instead of the expected 2.68. This is not a bug: it’s a result of the fact that most decimal fractions can’t be represented exactly as a float. See Floating Point Arithmetic: Issues and Limitations for more information.

If you really want to avoid this issue, you should be skipping the use of the built-in floating point objects with all their foibles, and instead opt for using the Decimal class.

You can then manipulate numbers in a great many ways with that while avoiding loss of precision. For example, the following transcript:

  • creates the exact value (not some closest floating point match);
  • changes the context so that it rounds half values away from zero (not up towards infinity as you may think from the ROUND_HALF_UP specifier) rather than using banker's rounding; then
  • rounds the value to two decimal places
>>> d = decimal.Decimal("59.925")  # Use string here, otherwise same problem.
>>> decimal.getcontext().rounding = decimal.ROUND_HALF_UP
>>> round(d, 2)
Decimal('59.93')

(1) Note that there is slightly different behaviour is the number is exactly halfway (such as 456.625, which can be represented exactly in IEEE-754). Python follows a round-halfway-to-even strategy in that case so it would go to 456.62 rather than 456.63.
